power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Humans use language to communicate psychological experiences.
Advancements in Natural Language Processing have enabled researchers to quantitatively study and assess psychological states and behaviors through language.
Insights from these language analyses are often best conveyed through visualizations.

Data-driven visualizations of how language statistically relates to psychological dimensions can help interpret assessment scores, uncover meaningful patterns, and understand the intricate relationships between language use and mental states.

Visualizations can be used to differentiate between related constructs (e.g., How does language related to depression versus anxiety differ?), understand the validity of assessment tools (e.g., Does the language related to high depression severity match with depression theory?), and explain language-based assessments (e.g., Which language is indicative of higher depression severity in a language-based assessment?).

This tutorial demonstrates how to transform language data into visual insights using the text and topics packages in R. We provide practical guidance on creating four types of visualizations based on different language analysis techniques, examining how language use patterns are statistically associated with psychological constructs.
We visualize 1) individual words and phrases (n-grams), 2) topics (word clusters), 3) words in the word embedding space, and 4) relevant language examples.
The different visualizations offer complementary perspectives, visualizing linguistic elements from individual words to overarching topics and text examples.
The underlying methods range from correlations between individual words to more advanced techniques, including topic modeling and Large Language Models.
By making these methods accessible, this tutorial aims to empower researchers to use language visualizations for meaningful, data-driven insights.
Language plays an important role in organising emotions and thoughts, as well as in sharing them with others and allowing us to comprehend the perspectives of others.
Through language, we make sense of past experiences, plan for the future, and navigate relationships by cooperating, learning, and teaching (Pennebaker et al., 2003; Tausczik & Pennebaker, 2010).

text.text: These diverse functions make language an integral part of human life.

Analyzing language use patterns can provide insights into how people express their states and traits and navigate their psychological experiences in diverse contexts (Boyd & Schwartz, 2021; Eichstaedt et al., 2021; Mihalcea et al., 2024).

text.text: Analyzing language use patterns-how people talk about emotions, thoughts, or experiences-can provide valuable insights into psychological constructs and behaviors.
Insights from language analyses are often best conveyed through visualizations.
Language visualizations enable researchers to explore and interpret the relationships between language use and psychological dimensions (e.g., Eichstaedt et al., 2021; Schwartz et al., 2013).

text.text: They can complement traditional statistical analyses, enhancing their interpretability and applicability, and uncover insights that might otherwise go unnoticed (e.g., O. Kjell et al., 2023; Nilsson et al., 2024).
text.formatted: They can complement traditional statistical analyses, enhancing their interpretability and applicability, and uncover insights that might otherwise go unnoticed (e.g., O. <ref type="bibr">Kjell et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Nilsson et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: With numerous language visualization options available, this tutorial aims to streamline quantitative techniques for a broader audience in a user-friendly manner through the R programming language.
Our aim is to support social and behavioural scientists in creating language visualizations and to advance the use of language visualizations for meaningful data-driven insights.
Visualizations of language can rely on different language analysis techniques.

There are different approaches to quantitative language analysis in psychology, which can roughly be divided into theorydriven and data-driven approaches (also known as closed-vocabulary and open-vocabulary approaches, respectively; Eichstaedt et al., 2021).
text.formatted: There are different approaches to quantitative language analysis in psychology, which can roughly be divided into theorydriven and data-driven approaches (also known as closed-vocabulary and open-vocabulary approaches, respectively; <ref type="bibr">Eichstaedt et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: A widely used theory-driven approach is the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC), which calculates the relative frequencies of predefined, psychologically relevant word dictionaries (e.g., negative emotion words, social words) across texts.
This enables the analysis of the relationships between word-dictionary frequencies and psychological states (Francis & Booth, 1993; Pennebaker et al., 2001).
text.formatted: This enables the analysis of the relationships between word-dictionary frequencies and psychological states <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Francis & Booth, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Pennebaker et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: However, data-driven approaches allow researchers to move beyond predefined categories to discover patterns directly from the data.
This often begins with ngrams, which are individual words or phrases (Schwartz et al., 2013).
text.formatted: This often begins with ngrams, which are individual words or phrases <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Schwartz et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: By identifying which specific words or phrases are statistically associated with a variable, researchers can capture linguistic markers that dictionaries might overlook.
To manage the vast variety of individual words, topic modeling (e.g., Latent Dirichlet Allocation; Blei et al., 2003) groups co-occurring words into clusters, or "topics."
text.formatted: To manage the vast variety of individual words, topic modeling (e.g., Latent Dirichlet Allocation; <ref type="bibr">Blei et al., 2003)</ref> groups co-occurring words into clusters, or "topics."

text.text: These word clusters can capture broader semantic themes that are often more stable and interpretable than individual words.
Over the past decade, advancements in Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Machine Learning (Devlin et al., 2019; Vaswani et al., 2017) have further transformed the field.

text.text: These technologies have made it possible to transform language into psychologically meaningful numerical representations called word embeddings, which can capture the complexities of language-such as context and word order-in a structured, quantified manner (Demszky et al., 2023; O. text.text: As these techniques grow more sophisticated, the role of visualization becomes critical, providing a necessary bridge between numerical outputs and interpretable psychological insights.

Beyond quantitatively analyzing language to produce assessment scores (e.g., depression severity scores based on language) or behavioural predictions (e.g., sick-leave predictions derived from text), language visualizations have emerged as a valuable complement to explore and elucidate individuals' experiences.
There are numerous reasons for using language visualizations, such as to better understand language data itself or to describe the measured constructs in more detail.
Visualizations can support the interpretation of assessment scores, reveal meaningful patterns, and clarify how language relates to psychological states and behaviours.
They offer intuitive ways to explore and communicate the output of language-based assessments, complementing quantitative scores with richer, more interpretable insights.

By visualizing language use based on statistically significant relationships, researchers can better understand individuals' psychological experiences and evaluate the validity of the tools used to assess them.

For example, language analyses complemented by visualizations have provided insights into how individuals' personality traits, gender, and age are expressed in social media language (e.g., Park et al., 2016; Schwartz et al., 2013) or how mental health descriptions vary with the severity of mental health issues (e.g., Gu et al., 2025; O. text.text: While these theoretical and empirical comparisons have identified the diverse applications and complementary nature of these techniques, practical guidance for their implementation remains limited.
In particular, while existing literature highlights opportunities for visualization, researchers often lack the technical guidance to create them.
This tutorial aims to fill this gap by providing practical guidance on different quantitative language analysis techniques, specifically tailored for making visualizations.

The tutorial uses R, specifically the topics package (Ackermann et al., 2024) and the text package (O. Kjell et al., 2023), and provides step-by-step guidance for making a range of data-driven language visualizations.

text.text: Drawing on the aforementioned literature, we offer user-friendly tools, sensible defaults, and practical "rules of thumb" intended as helpful starting points rather than strict prescriptions.
This guidance is designed to support researchers in making informed decisions and thoughtful applications without requiring deep technical expertise.

Here, we visualize individual words and phrases (also called n-grams) in relation to a variable of interest.

Specifically, we visualize individual words (from the depression and worry responses) positively and negatively associated with depression severity (PHQ-9 ratings) through two differential word clouds.

The analyses underlying this visualization involve structuring meaningful n-grams based on word frequency and co-occurrence, and testing the relationship between the n-gram frequencies and PHQ-9 ratings using regression.

The visualization is created with three functions of the topics package, including 1) topicsGrams(), which structures meaningful n-grams; 2) topicsTest(), which significance tests the n-grams in relation to the variable of interest; and last, 3) topicsPlot(), which visualizes the significant n-grams.
Table 3 at the end of the tutorial provides rules of thumb and recommendations for setting the parameters across functions.

text.text: Participants' responses are first split into individual words and phrases (n-grams) using the topicsGrams() function.
N-grams are sequences of words: One-grams are single words, and 2-or 3grams are sequences of words combined with underscores (e.g., "happy_birthday" instead of "happy" and "birthday").
The size of n-grams is set with the ngram_window parameter (here, set to sequences of 1 to 3 words).
Rather than including all possible 2-and 3-grams, it is possible to only retain phrases from which the individual words are more likely to occur together than to occur independently.
This is achieved using the pmi_threshold parameter (set to 5 here), based on the Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI; Church & Hanks, 1990; Lin, 1998; Schwartz et al., 2013).
text.formatted: This is achieved using the pmi_threshold parameter (set to 5 here), based on the Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI; <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Church & Hanks, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Lin, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Schwartz et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: The PMI quantifies the association between two events -in the context of n-grams, these events correspond to words that co-occur.
When two words co-occur more often than expected by chance, the PMI of the phrase will be larger than 0.
When the two words occur together purely by chance (i.e., they are independent), the PMI of the phrase will be 0.
Phrases with a PMI greater than 1 occur at least twice as likely as expected by chance.

Using the PMI is a common method for removing weak or less meaningful associations and limiting the correction for multiple comparisons in subsequent statistical tests (Lin, 1998; Schwartz et al., 2013; see Table 3 for rules of thumb).
text.formatted: Using the PMI is a common method for removing weak or less meaningful associations and limiting the correction for multiple comparisons in subsequent statistical tests <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Lin, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Schwartz et al., 2013</ref>; see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">3</ref> for rules of thumb).

text.text: To further ensure focus on meaningful n-grams and limit the corrections for multiple comparisons, it is possible to restrict the analyses to words and phrases used by a minimum proportion of the participant sample (e.g., see Atkins et al., 2012; Eichstaedt et al., 2021) using the occurance_rate parameter (here, set to 0.01, which limits the analysis to n-grams that appear in at least 1% of individuals' responses; see Table 3 for rules of thumb).

text.text: The n-grams are filtered based on their frequency of occurrence to include only those n-grams that appear in a certain proportion of the responses, calculated by dividing the number of responses that contain a specific n-gram by the total number of responses.
Additionally, it is possible to remove words using the stopwords parameter.

Here, you can specify a list of common words (such as "the", "and", "is") that you want to exclude from the analysis, because they are not expected to be meaningful in relation to the variable of interest (e.g., depression severity).
The default option is the predefined list of 175 stopwords from the snowball lexicon (Porter, 2001).
text.formatted: The default option is the predefined list of 175 stopwords from the snowball lexicon <ref type="bibr">(Porter, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: By removing stopwords, the function focuses on more meaningful words and phrases, enhancing the clarity and relevance of the resulting visualizations.

Before the responses are structured into n-grams, the responses are preprocessed according to parameter settings (which defaults to TRUE), including lower (texts are lowercased), remove_punctuation (punctuation is removed), and remove_numbers (numbers are removed).
The output of topicsGrams() is a list of the most frequently occurring n-grams across the dataset, including their frequency, prevalence, and the number of documents.

The frequency indicates the number of times an n-gram appears in the dataset; the prevalence indicates the frequency of an n-gram relative to the total number of n-grams in the dataset; and the number of documents indicates the number of distinct responses in which an n-gram appears.

We examine which n-grams are statistically related to a variable of interest (here, depression severity) using the topicsTest() function (this function can also be used to statistically test word clusters [topics], which will be described in the next visualization).
The output of the topicsGrams() function is submitted to the ngrams parameter, and the variable of interest to the x_variable parameter.

We control for age and gender using the controls parameter and correct for multiple comparisons using the p_adjust_method parameter (here, the default method, False Discovery Rate ["fdr"]; Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995).
text.formatted: We control for age and gender using the controls parameter and correct for multiple comparisons using the p_adjust_method parameter (here, the default method, False Discovery Rate ["fdr"]; <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: The method for testing the statistical relationship is specified by the test_method parameter.
The default in topicsTest() is to perform multiple regression ("linear_regression" when the outcome is continuous or "logistic_regression" when the outcome is binary).
In this case, we conduct a multiple regression using:

Where z ( depression _ severity ) is the standardized depression rating scale; z ( ngram 1 _ freq ) is the standardized frequency of the n-gram; β 0 is the intercept of the regression model; β 1 , β 2 and β 3 are the coefficients (standardized beta coefficients) representing the unique contributions of the tested n-gram, age, gender, with depression severity, respectively; and ϵ is the error term.

This regression produces standardized beta coefficients (β), where the beta coefficient can be interpreted as a controlled (partial) correlation, indicating the unique association between each predictor and the z ( wor d 1 _ freq ).
For example, the beta of z ( depression _ severity ) in this model reflects the unique association of depression severity with n-gram 1, controlling for age and gender.
Other variables in the output list include the (adjusted) p-values (i.e., corrected for multiple comparisons) and the prevalence of each n-gram.
Finally, we create the visualization by plotting the differential word clouds using the topicsPlot() function.
Here, the n-grams of topicsGrams() are submitted to the ngrams parameter, and the significant test results of topicsTest() to the test parameter.

The n-grams are selected based on the strength of the relationship with depression severity (β) through the ngram_select parameter (default is estimate, but can be changed to select based on prevalence).

The colours of the n-grams in the two word clouds are set with the color_scheme parameter (here, orange indicating a negative association and blue indicating a positive association with depression severity; see Table 3 for rules of thumb).

The word clouds are accompanied by two legends: one indicating the strength of each n-gram's relationship with depression severity (β) via a colour gradient, and one indicating the prevalence of each n-gram by font size.

The visualization components (i.e., word clouds and legends) can be saved and imported into programs of choice, such as PowerPoint or Google Drawings, to combine them and refine the figures and layout (see the Supplementary Material for a step-by-step overview).

Here, we visualize topics (word clusters) in relation to a variable of interest.
Topic visualizations cluster words into semantically meaningful themes, offering a higher-level summary of language patterns that may not be apparent from individual words alone.
Specifically, we visualize topics (in the depression and worry responses) positively and negatively associated with depression severity (PHQ-9 ratings) through multiple topic word clouds.

The analyses underlying these visualizations involve extracting underlying topics from the responses using topic modelling and testing the relationship between these topics and the PHQ-9 ratings using regression.

There exist different topic modelling techniques, such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA; Blei et al., 2003), Structural Topic Modelling (STM; Roberts et al., 2014), and BERTopic (Grootendorst, 2022).
text.formatted: There exist different topic modelling techniques, such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA; <ref type="bibr">Blei et al., 2003)</ref>, Structural Topic Modelling (STM; <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Roberts et al., 2014)</ref>, and BERTopic <ref type="bibr">(Grootendorst, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: They share the same aim of automatically identifying themes in text.

LDA is a probabilistic model that can be used to uncover underlying topics within text collections by modelling texts as mixtures of topics and topics as distributions over words (Blei et al., 2003; Griffiths et al., 2007).
text.formatted: LDA is a probabilistic model that can be used to uncover underlying topics within text collections by modelling texts as mixtures of topics and topics as distributions over words <ref type="bibr">(Blei et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Griffiths et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: STM is similar to LDA but extends the probabilistic modelling by allowing text-level metadata (e.g., time, authorship, or demographics) to influence the topic prevalence and content (Roberts et al., 2014; 2019), requiring more decisions and setup.
text.formatted: STM is similar to LDA but extends the probabilistic modelling by allowing text-level metadata (e.g., time, authorship, or demographics) to influence the topic prevalence and content <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Roberts et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">2019)</ref>, requiring more decisions and setup.

text.text: BERTopic, in contrast, is a more recent method that instead of relying on word frequency and co-occurrence, leverages Large Language Models to generate topic representations.
This method uses word embeddings-numerical representations of word meaning derived from Large Language Models.
Topics are derived from clustering word embeddings to capture word meanings in a contextualized way (Grootendorst, 2022).
text.formatted: Topics are derived from clustering word embeddings to capture word meanings in a contextualized way <ref type="bibr">(Grootendorst, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This tutorial focuses on LDA and BERTopic because together they illustrate two complementary perspectives: a foundational, more interpretable probabilistic approach and a more modern embedding-based method.
See Egger & Yu (2022) for a more detailed comparison between different topic modeling approaches, and see the stm package and tutorial (Roberts et al., 2019) for an introduction to STM.
text.formatted: See <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Egger & Yu (2022)</ref> for a more detailed comparison between different topic modeling approaches, and see the stm package and tutorial <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Roberts et al., 2019)</ref> for an introduction to STM.

text.text: LDA topics are clusters of co-occurring words within a collection of texts or responses, identified using the LDA algorithm.

The identification and visualization of the LDA topics is conducted through five functions of the topics package: 1) topicsDtm(), which creates a matrix of the text data (here, the depression and worry responses), 2) topicsModel(), which employs the LDA algorithm to identify underlying topics within the matrix, 3) topicsAssess(), which applies the trained LDA model to assign relative frequencies of each topic on the specified language data, 4) topicsTest(), which significance tests the topic frequencies in relation to individuals' characteristics (here, depression severity), and 5) topicsPlot(), which visualizes the significant topics.
We use the topicsDtm() function to structure participants' responses into a Document Term Matrix (DTM).
A DTM represents the frequencies of the n-grams across all responses and serves as the primary input for the LDA algorithm.
By transforming language responses into a structured matrix, the DTM enables the efficient application of algorithms such as LDA to uncover underlying topics.

The matrix is constructed by processing the text data, which includes removing stopwords (using the stopwords parameter), structuring n-grams (with the ngram_window parameter), and filtering n-grams based on specified thresholds using the pmi_threshold and occurance_rate parameters, as described in the previous visualization.
Also, the same preprocessing parameters apply (e.g., lower, remove_punctuation, and remove_numbers).

# Structure the depression and worry responses into a DTM topics_DTM <-topicsDtm( data = dep_wor_language$Language, ngram_window = c(1, 3), # Allow for n-grams of 1 to 3 words stopwords = stopwords<:stopwords("en", source = "snowball"), # Remove stopwords pmi_threshold = 5, # Set the PMI threshold to 5 occurance_rate = 0.01) # Set occurrence rate to 1% #Output: Matrix including the frequencies of the most frequent n-grams across all responses To understand and evaluate the created DTM, it can be inspected using the topicsDtmEval() function, which provides an overview of the frequencies of n-grams in the matrix (i.e., how many responses each n-gram appears in).

Removing stop words (or other highly frequent words) is recommended since LDA does not handle common words very well: The frequency of the most frequent words should not differ too much from the frequency of the second most frequent word.

It is possible to remove the most and/or least frequent words from the DTM by setting a frequency threshold using the removal_mode (including removal_rate_most and removal_rate_least) parameters in the topicsDtm() function (see Table 3 for rules of thumb and the Supplementary Material for applying these parameters when analyzing longer text entries).

Once the DTM is established, we employ the LDA algorithm to identify underlying topics within the text data using the topicsModel() 1 function.
LDA assumes that texts are mixtures of topics, and each topic is characterized by a distribution over words.

Using techniques such as Gibbs sampling (Yao et al., 2009), an underlying topic structure is inferred by estimating 1) the topic prevalences for each response and 2) the word distributions for each topic.
text.formatted: Using techniques such as Gibbs sampling <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Yao et al., 2009)</ref>, an underlying topic structure is inferred by estimating 1) the topic prevalences for each response and 2) the word distributions for each topic.

text.text: In essence, Gibbs sampling is a repetitive process that iteratively reassigns words to topics until the most likely overall topic structure emerges.

Notably, LDA requires pre-specifying the number of topics, which can be challenging and may not always capture the actual underlying structure of the data (a rough rule of thumb is one topic per 50 responses; see Table 3).

The output contains a summary of all topics, including their label, top terms, coherence, and prevalence.

The label indicates the most dominant or representative word in the cluster, and the top terms show the most representative words for each topic (of which the number of words is set with the num_top_words parameter, default is 10).
These variables help define what the topic is "about".
The coherence metric indicates how semantically related the top terms in a topic are, with higher values indicating more coherent and interpretable topics.
These scores represent the average PMI across all pairs of words in a topic and range from 0 to 1.
Finally, prevalence indicates the proportion of responses in which the topic appears (i.e., relative frequencies), as described in the previous visualization.
It is possible to visualize the most prevalent topics in the trained LDA model using the topicsPlot() function.

Next, the trained LDA model is applied to estimate the relative frequencies of the topics (i.e., their prevalence) in the participants' responses using the topicsAssess() function.
Here, the output of topicsModel() is submitted to the model parameter, and the responses to the data parameter.
The output is a table showing the estimated relative frequencies for each topic.
The rows represent the language responses, the columns represent the topics, and the values indicate the proportion of each topic within the corresponding language response.
It is also possible to submit new text data to the data parameter (i.e., not used for training the LDA model).
Applying the model to "unseen" language is useful for evaluating the model's generalizability and for applying the discovered topics to additional data.
The function ensures that the new data are compatible with the existing DTM format and infers their topic distributions.
To examine which topics are statistically related to the variable of interest (here, depression severity), we used topicsTest() as previously described in the previous visualization.
Here, the estimated frequencies of topicsAssess() are submitted to the preds parameter, and the LDA model of topicsModel() is submitted to the model parameter.

The output also includes the (adjusted) p-values and the prevalence and coherence of each topic.

BERTopic (Grootendorst, 2022) is a more recent topic modeling method that instead of relying on word frequency and co-occurrence like LDA, uses word embeddings from Large Language Models to group semantically similar texts into topics.
text.formatted: BERTopic <ref type="bibr">(Grootendorst, 2022)</ref> is a more recent topic modeling method that instead of relying on word frequency and co-occurrence like LDA, uses word embeddings from Large Language Models to group semantically similar texts into topics.

text.text: The identification and visualization of the BERTopics is conducted through three functions of the text package: 1) textTopics(), which leverages a pretrained Large Language Models to generate topic representations of the text (here, the depression and worry responses), 2) textTopicsTest(), which significance tests the topic representations in relation to individuals' characteristics (here, depression severity), and 5) textTopicsWordcloud(), which visualizes the significant topics.
The textTopics() function generates topic representations of the depression and worry responses, including 1-to 3-grams (the default in n_gram_range).
This function employs a pre-trained Large Language Model from the Huggingface library to convert the words into word embeddings.
The language model (here, the default model "distilroberta-base"; Sanh et al., 2019) is submitted to the embedding_model parameter, and the text data is submitted to the variable_name parameter.
text.formatted: The language model (here, the default model "distilroberta-base"; <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Sanh et al., 2019)</ref> is submitted to the embedding_model parameter, and the text data is submitted to the variable_name parameter.

text.text: A word embedding is a vector that numerically represents the meaning of a word.
Since word embeddings comprise many numbers, a word is represented by many dimensions.
By applying the pre-trained word embeddings from the Large Language Model, each response is converted into a high-dimensional embedding.

Next, the embeddings are reduced in dimensionality, and the reduced embeddings are clustered by applying two different clustering algorithms: the Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP; McInnes et al., 2018) for dimensionality reduction and the Hierarchical Density-Based Spatial Clustering (HBDSCAN; McInnes et al., 2017) for clustering.

text.text: Unlike LDA, the function does not require prespecifying the number of topics, and it does not return topic prevalences because it is based on embeddings rather than word frequencies and co-occurrences.

The number of top terms per topic representation is set with the num_top_words parameter (default is 10).
Then, the trained BERTopics model is submitted to the textTopicsTest() function to perform a significance test of the topic representations in relation to depression severity.

The depression ratings are submitted to the x_variable parameter, and the method for testing the statistical relation is set with the test_method parameter (here, the default is "linear regression" since the target variable is continuous).

Multiple regression is applied while controlling for age and gender (set with the controls parameter) and correcting for multiple comparisons using the False Discovery Rate (FDR) procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995; set with the p_adjust_method parameter).

Here, we visualize words in the word embedding space in relation to a variable of interest.

Specifically, we visualize individual words (from the depression and worry responses) positively and negatively associated with depression severity (PHQ-9 ratings) using the Supervised Dimension Projection method (Kjell et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Specifically, we visualize individual words (from the depression and worry responses) positively and negatively associated with depression severity (PHQ-9 ratings) using the Supervised Dimension Projection method <ref type="bibr">(Kjell et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: While visualizations of n-grams and LDA topics provide insights based on word frequency and co-occurrence, visualizing words in the word embedding space offers a more semantic perspective.
Similarly to BERTopic, the analyses underlying this visualization make use of word embeddings.

By projecting these embeddings onto a supervised dimension (e.g., low to high depression severity), we can visualize which words are most semantically aligned with higher or lower levels of the outcome of interest.
This approach can capture patterns in word use that may not be evident through frequency-based methods alone and provides a complement to more traditional techniques like n-gram or topic analyses.
As discussed previously, a word embedding is a vector that numerically represents the meaning of a word.
Since word embeddings comprise many numbers, a word is represented by many dimensions in the word embedding space.

The numbers can be seen as coordinates in a high-dimensional space: The closer two words are in this space, the more similar their word embeddings are, and the more similar the words are expected to be in meaning.

The Supervised Dimension Projection plot can be created with three functions of the text package, including 1) textEmbed(), which creates word embeddings of the participants' responses, 2) textProjection(), which preprocesses the data for plotting by creating supervised dimension projections, and 3) textProjectionPlot(), which visualizes the words in the word embedding space.
The functions are described below; see the tutorial of the text-package for more detailed descriptions (O. Kjell et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The functions are described below; see the tutorial of the text-package for more detailed descriptions (O. <ref type="bibr">Kjell et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: We transformed the language responses into word embeddings using the textEmbed() function, which employs a pre-trained Large Language Model from the Huggingface library.

While many models exist (the default is BERT; "bert-base-uncased"; Devlin et al., 2019), we here use the MixedBread model ("mixedbread-ai"; Li & Li, 2023), which has shown good performance in psychological assessment tasks (e.g., Bång et al., in revision).
text.formatted: While many models exist (the default is BERT; "bert-base-uncased"; <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Devlin et al., 2019)</ref>, we here use the MixedBread model ("mixedbread-ai"; <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Li & Li, 2023)</ref>, which has shown good performance in psychological assessment tasks (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Bång et al., in revision)</ref>.

text.text: The name of the language model is submitted to the model parameter, and the language responses are submitted to the texts parameter.
Before the responses are transformed into embeddings, the language is preprocessed by removing Non-ASCII characters (remove_non_ascii = TRUE), since most language models cannot handle these well.
ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) characters include the English alphabet, numbers, and some basic punctuation.
The responses are first split into individual words, where every single word of each response gets its own embedding.
The output of the function comprises three types of contextualised embeddings, which represent the meaning of the words in their context.

These types of embeddings are 1) token embeddings, which represent the meaning of a single word or word stem (e.g., "someone" consists of the tokens "some" and "one") in a specific response, 2) text embeddings, which represent the meaning of a response by combining all token embeddings of the response, and 3) word type embeddings, which represent the meaning of a word type by combining all token embeddings of a word.
A word type refers to a word in general (i.e., in all responses) as opposed to a token, which refers to a word in a specific response.
The Supervised Dimension Projection requires two types of embeddings as input, namely the text and word type embeddings.
The text embeddings are created by taking the mean of all token embeddings in a specific response (with the aggregation_from_tokens_to_texts parameter).
The word type embeddings are created by taking the mean of all token embeddings for a specific word (with the aggregation_from_tokens_to_word_types parameter).

# Transform the language into word embeddings # Apply pre-trained word embeddings to transform the responses into word embeddings embeddings <-textEmbed( texts = dep_wor_language$Language, model = "mixedbread-ai/mxbai-embed-large-v1", # Large Language Model aggregation_from_tokens_to_texts = "mean", # Combine token embeddings into text embeddings aggregation_from_tokens_to_word_types = "mean", # Combine token embeddings into word type embeddings keep_token_embeddings = FALSE) # Do not save token embeddings #Output: Contextual embeddings of the language responses # Save the word embeddings considering this analysis takes time to compute saveRDS(embeddings, "embeddings.rds")

text.text: The embeddings are analysed in relation to different values of the variable of interest (here, depression severity) using the textProjection() function.
This function employs the Supervised Dimension Projection, which involves creating an embedding that captures the distinction between high and low depression severity.
The language responses are submitted to the words parameter, and the variable of interest (here, depression severity) to the x parameter.
The text and word type embeddings of the textEmbed() function are submitted to the word_embeddings and word_types_embeddings parameters.
It is also possible to test and visualize the words in relation to two variables of interest (see

To create an embedding that captures the distinction between high and low depression severity, the function divides the dataset into two groups based on a split (default is median) of the depression rating scale, resulting in a high and low-scoring group.

The embeddings of the two groups are subtracted from each other to create an embedding that captures the distinction between high and low depression severity, also known as the supervised dimension in the word embedding space.
Next, supervised dimension projections are created by projecting each single word embedding onto this supervised dimension.
This is achieved by using the dot product, which mathematically measures how similar two embeddings are.

To determine the statistical significance of the created supervised dimension projections, they are compared to a null distribution of supervised dimension projections while correcting for multiple comparisons to obtain a p-value.
Finally, we create the Supervised Dimension Projection plot using the textProjectionPlot() function.
The preprocessed data from the textProjection() function are submitted to the word_data parameter.
Other parameters make it possible to correct for multiple comparisons (p_adjust_method) and remove words not to be plotted (remove_words).
The layout of the plot can be refined with various aesthethics parameters, such as setting colours (bivariate_color_codes) and adjusting the font size (word_size_range).

Here, we present relevant text examples from the language data in relation to different variables of interest.
Specifically, we visualize example responses to the depression and worry questions in relation to a) n-gram user frequencies, b) topic prevalences, and c) language-based assessed depression severity.
It can be useful to visualize complete responses, because words on their own can be ambiguous and open to multiple interpretations.
Their meaning often depends on contextespecially when describing psychological experiences.
To reduce this ambiguity, it is useful to visualize not just isolated words or topics but examples of complete responses or texts.
These richer units of language help clarify what is being expressed, how words or topics are embedded in the raw language data, and how they relate to psychological constructs.
Combining data-driven insights with qualitative interpretations can enable a deeper exploration of the narrative contexts that drive the broader statistical trends.
To exemplify, we will here show the responses with a) the highest user frequencies of the n-gram "lack" (see Figure 1) and b) the highest prevalences of the topic "feeling" (see Figure 4).

text.text: We also visualize responses that exemplify the highest language-based assessments of depression severity to demonstrate how such examples can provide insight into a model's performance and validity.
When training a model to assess a psychological construct, there exist several metrics to evaluate its performance.
Here, we train a model on the depression and worry responses to assess the participants' PHQ-9 ratings.

To evaluate performance, we can compute the correlation (r) between the languagebased assessed and targeted scores or calculate the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) -the average absolute difference between the assessed and targeted scores in PHQ scale units.

To evaluate the model beyond these numerical summaries, we can identify the responses of the participants that the model identifies as having, for example, the lowest or the highest depression severity.

When the linguistic content of these responses matches established psychological theories or clinical judgment, this can provide evidence of face validity and offers a more nuanced understanding of the model's behavior than a single number can provide.

The analyses underlying these visualizations of language examples include identifying the language responses with the a) highest user frequencies of the n-gram "lack", b) highest estimated prevalences of the topic "feeling", and c) highest language-based assessed depression severity.
These examples are identified and visualized using the textExamples() function of the text package.

For the language-based assessed depression severity, first two other functions of the text package are employed, namely textEmbed(), which creates word embeddings of the language responses, and textTrain(), which creates a language-based based assessment model by training the word embeddings to assess the depression severity scores.
To be able to visualize language examples based on their language-based assessed depression severity, we first need to train a language-based assessment model.

The language-based assessment model is created using the already created text embeddings of the responses from the textEmbed() function, as previously described in the visualization of words in the word embedding space.
We examine the relationship between the word embeddings and the depression severity scores using the textTrain() function.
Here, a language-based assessment model is trained using the word embeddings as predictors and the participant's PHQ ratings as target scores.
The text embeddings from textEmbed() are submitted to the x parameter, and the target variable (here, depression severity) to the y parameter.
The default applies ridge regression, an advanced form of multiple linear regression that reduces the impact of irrelevant predictors through a penalty.
This is useful, since word embeddings consists of a high number of dimensions (i.e., predictor variables).

To find the right penalty (i.e., how much the impact of irrelevant predictors is reduced) and avoid overfitting the data (i.e., how generalisable the model is to new data), nested 10-fold cross-validation is applied.
For a more detailed description of the textTrain() function, see the text tutorial (O. Kjell et al., 2023).

We here present three examples of how to make two-dimensional visualizations (i.e., in relation to variables of interest), including LDA topics, words in the word embedding space, and language examples.

We visualize the LDA topics and the words in the word embedding space in relation to the same two variables of interest: the type of language response (i.e., depression versus worry) and depression severity.

While one-dimensional plots reveal how language relates to a single psychological variable, two-dimensional visualizations offer a richer view by simultaneously illustrating how words or topics differ across both variables.
This can help to disentangle overlapping constructs (e.g., worry and depression) and identify language that is specific to one versus both.

Such visualizations are especially useful when psychological states are correlated (e.g., comorbid disorders) or when researchers are interested in both condition-specific and severity-related language features.

The two-dimensional visualization of topics is created using the previously created DTM and LDA model using topicsDtm(), topicsModel(), and topicsAssess() as described in the onedimensional visualization of LDA topics.
The previously described topicsTest() function is used to examine which topics are statistically related to depression severity and type of language (depression versus worry responses).
The indicator for depression versus worry language is submitted to the x_variable parameter, and the depression rating scale is submitted to the y_variable parameter 3 .
The default in topicsTest() applies multiple regression.

Here, linear regression is applied to assess the continuous outcome (i.e., the PHQ-9 ratings) and logistic regression is applied to assess the binary outcome (i.e., the depression [0] versus worry [1] indicator), while controlling for age and gender.

The output consists of standardized beta coefficients, indicating the unique associations between each topic and depression severity, and log odds, indicating the probability of the topic being from worry versus depression language.
The significance tests and the LDA model are submitted to the earlier described topicsPlot() function to produce topic word clouds.

text.text: While a benefit of language visualizations is their intuitive communication, interpreting language visualizations warrants some considerations.
A key difference between, for example, interpreting rating scale scores versus language lies in dimensionality (Ganesan et al., 2021; Stochl et al., 2022).

text.text: Validated scales, such as the PHQ-9, are often one-dimensional (e.g., from low to high depression severity; Kroenke et al., 2001), whereas language visualizations comprise language features with multiple dimensions (e.g., calm has positive valence and low arousal).

text.text: Language analyses involve a significantly higher number of units: They may examine tens, hundreds, or even thousands of words, phrases, or topics, including additional complexities such as polysemy (i.e., words may have multiple meanings depending on the context; Nerlich, 2003) and subtleties in language use (e.g., sarcasm, idioms, cultural expressions; Reyes et al., 2012).

text.text: Because of these complexities, language visualizations require thoughtful interpretations to identify higher-order patterns and relationships.
Below, we present factors to consider when interpreting language visualizations, followed by ethical considerations.
We recommend considering different visualization methods collectively or complementing the language visualizations with other methodological approaches for a comprehensive understanding.
Triangulation of methods can lead to more robust conclusions, ensuring that findings are not an artefact of any single technique (Lahat et al., 2015; Lawlor et al., 2016).

text.text: Visualizations of single words (e.g., words in the word embedding space) can benefit from visualizations of topics, because word clusters can provide more context.

For example, the n-gram plot (Figure 1) visualizes the word "pointless" as related to higher depression severity, and we can see in the BERtopics plot (Figure 5) that it is part of the same cluster as "suicide", "alive_selfish" and "life_boring", which provides context to positive association with depression severity.

text.text: Anchor in context and theoretical frameworks.
Contextualisation is essential for interpreting language visualizations.
For example, instead of overinterpreting single words or topics, it is more suitable to find overarching themes and contextualise them with theoretical frameworks and other empirical findings.
Contextualization can help identify higher-order patterns and avoid potential biases in interpretation.
For example, the prominence of a word in a word cloud may suggest it is important, but its significance could be influenced by confounding factors that are not immediately apparent.
For example, the word "depressed" can be part of one of the topics related to low depression severity, such as in combination with the use of a negation before.
Similarly, the words "interest" or "motivation" might be visualized in association with high depression severity.

Contextualisation might provide cooccurrences with words like "lack" or "loss", which together fit theoretical frameworks and diagnostic criteria of depression (e.g., anhedonia; American Psychiatric Association [APA], 2013).

It is crucial to carefully consider the thematic and contextual implications, rather than equating linguistic patterns directly with psychological states, to ensure that insights are meaningful and valid.
Consider the language source.

To contextualize language visualizations, it is essential to consider where the language originated (e.g., social media, survey responses, interview transcripts), as the context in which it was generated can significantly impact its patterns.
For example, responses to a question such as "Over the last 2 weeks, have you been depressed or not?"
might have a higher chance of including words such as "depressed", "not", and "yes" or "no" than, for example, social media posts.
Also, the length of the text entries can influence the results, as we elaborate on in the Supplementary Material, where we apply the analyses to essays instead of survey responses.

Furthermore, it is essential to consider the authors' demographics and cultural background, as these factors significantly influence individuals' language patterns (Abitbol et al., 2018; Rai et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Furthermore, it is essential to consider the authors' demographics and cultural background, as these factors significantly influence individuals' language patterns <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abitbol et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Rai et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: It is essential to consider that research aims and design influence how visualizations can be interpreted, such as whether they are created in the context of exploratory analyses (e.g., identifying patterns and generating hypotheses) or confirmatory analyses (e.g., testing specific hypotheses or relationships).
It is important to state this explicitly, since language has many features, and some words or topics might almost always be significant.
One approach is to compute topics and, before any further analysis, pre-register the topics hypothesized to relate to the outcome, then test them on a new dataset (e.g., see O. Kjell et al., 2024).

text.text: For instance, a patient using more sadnessrelated topics in their language does not necessarily mean the patient is more depressed clinically, as depression is a multifaceted construct with specific diagnostic criteria (APA, 2013), including loss of interest, sleep problems, and so on, and language patterns alone may only partially reflect these criteria.

Therefore, interpreting the statistical significance or meaning of a topic differs from interpreting a rating scale score or the frequency of a theory-driven word dictionary from the LIWC, where the meaning has been predefined rather than retrieved from a data-driven approach.
Consider effect sizes carefully.
Finally, interpreting effect sizes, for example, for topics requires some considerations.

In general, effect sizes are often misinterpreted due to an overreliance on general effect size benchmarks that were not intended for broad application across various research fields (Glaser et al., 2025).

This is because the signal in language is spread out, and thus, any single word or topic usually has a small signal.
These signals become stronger when considered together.

text.text: Privacy and Data Sensitivity.
Language data often contains personal and sensitive information.
Even when anonymised, certain linguistic patterns can indirectly reveal identifying details.

Therefore, it is essential to respect the privacy and sensitivity of the data, especially when the language relates to personal or clinical topics, and consider in each analysis which parts are identifiable (alone or in combination) and what can be saved or shared (and how).
Researchers should ensure that data collection and analysis comply with established ethical guidelines, including obtaining informed consent and implementing secure data storage practices.
AI-based techniques and language-based assessments can inherit and amplify biases present in training data.
For example, gender, racial, or socio-economic biases may manifest in word associations, leading to misleading conclusions (Giorgi et al., 2022).
text.formatted: For example, gender, racial, or socio-economic biases may manifest in word associations, leading to misleading conclusions <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Giorgi et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Researchers are recommended to critically examine their models for bias and consider using debiasing techniques when necessary, such as controlling for certain characteristics (e.g., age and gender) and visualizing these controls.
Language visualizations summarise complex, high-dimensional data into intuitive formats, such as topics.

This simplification makes results more accessible and generalisable but also risks obscuring critical nuances, especially if the visualization design introduces bias or fails to highlight key patterns or critical details (Egger & Yu, 2022).
text.formatted: This simplification makes results more accessible and generalisable but also risks obscuring critical nuances, especially if the visualization design introduces bias or fails to highlight key patterns or critical details <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Egger & Yu, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Overgeneralised interpretations may lead to misleading conclusions or stigmatisation.

Researchers are advised to emphasize that visualization results represent data-driven behavioral patterns, which are probabilistic rather than deterministic, and can be best interpreted within the context of theoretical frameworks, other empirical findings, and complementary methods.
Given the complexity of quantitative language analyses using Natural Language Processing and Large Language Models, ensuring transparency in methodological choices is important.

Consider providing clear documentation on how data was processed, which parameters were used, and how visualizations were generated, which enhances reproducibility and allows for critical evaluation by other researchers.

This tutorial has introduced four complementary types of language visualizations, which can be created with the topics and text packages in R. Each method-word-level analysis, topic modelling, word embeddings, and identifying relevant text examples-offers unique insights into the relationship between language use patterns and psychological constructs.
We recommend using different visualizations together, taking context and theory into account for interpretation.

By integrating robust methodological practices with ethical responsibility, this tutorial aims to support social and behavioral scientists in creating language visualizations and advancing their use for meaningful, data-driven insights.
To practice creating different types of visualizations, we encourage readers to follow the tutorial steps using their own data or other variables from the dep_wor_data set.

The code blocks below present how to make visualizations of words and phrases (n-grams).
Specifically, we visualize individual words (from the essays) that are positively or negatively associated with valence using two differential word clouds.

The analyses underlying this visualization involve structuring meaningful n-grams based on word frequency and co-occurrence, and testing the relationship between the n-gram frequencies and valence scores using regression.

As described previously, the visualization is created with three functions of the topics package, including 1) topicsGrams(), which structures meaningful n-grams; 2) topicsTest(), which significance tests the n-grams in relation to the variable of interest; and last, 3) topicsPlot(), which visualizes the significant n-grams.
Students' essays are first split into individual words and phrases (n-grams) using the topicsGrams() function.
Compared to the visualizations of the depression and worry responses, we lowered the pmi_threshold to 3 (instead of 5) since our dataset is larger (i.e., longer text entries).

As previously described, the Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) threshold is used to ensure that the n-grams (or word clusters in case of topics) we visualize are statistically meaningful associations rather than random co-occurrences (Schwartz et al., 2013).
text.formatted: As previously described, the Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) threshold is used to ensure that the n-grams (or word clusters in case of topics) we visualize are statistically meaningful associations rather than random co-occurrences <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Schwartz et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: In short or probed responses, the limited vocabulary makes word co-occurrences more dense and obvious.
However, in longer texts, people use a wider variety of words.
If the threshold remains too high for long-form text, meaningful but less-frequent semantic patterns might be filtered out as "noise".

text.text: Specifically, we visualize topics (from the essays) that are positively or negatively associated with valence using multiple topic word clouds.
LDA topics are clusters of frequently co-occurring words within a collection of texts or responses.
The analyses underlying this visualization involve extracting topics using the LDA algorithm and testing the relationship between these topics and valence scores using regression.

As described previously, we identify and visualize the topics through five functions of the topics package: 1) topicsDtm(), which creates a matrix of the text data (here, essays), 2) topicsModel(), which employs the LDA algorithm to identify underlying topics within the matrix, 3) topicsPreds(), which applies the trained LDA model to assign relative frequencies of each topic on the specified language data, 4) topicsTest(), which significance tests the topic frequencies in relation to individuals' characteristics (here, valence), and 5) topicsPlot(), which visualizes the significant topics.

We use the topicsDtm() function to structure the essays into a Document Term Matrix (DTM), which represents the relative frequencies of the n-grams and serves as the primary input for the LDA algorithm.
As in the previous visualization of n-grams, we lowered the pmi_threshold to 3 (instead of 5) because the essay data consist of longer text entries than the depression and worry responses.
To understand and evaluate the created DTM, we use the topicsDtmEval() function to obtain an overview of the ngram frequencies in the matrix.

text.text: We apply the LDA algorithm to this updated DTM using the topicsModel() function to identify underlying topics.
Since our essay data set includes longer text entries as compared to the depression and worry responses, we optimize for 30 instead of 20 topics (set with the num_topics parameter).
Short responses, especially the answers to targeted questions, are most likely to include a few broad themes.

In contrast, longer narratives (e.g., stream-of-consciousness essays in which individuals write about their current thoughts) are more likely to cover multiple distinct ideas, subthemes, and nuances within a single text.
After identifying 30 topics, we visualize the most prevalent topics in the trained LDA model using the topicsPlot() function.
The output of the topicsModel() function contains a summary of all topics, including their label, top terms, coherence, and prevalence.
The prevalence indicates the proportion of responses in which the topic appears (i.e., the relative frequencies).

text.text: Instead of relying on word frequency and co-occurrence, BERTopic uses word embeddings from Large Language Models to group semantically similar texts into topics.

As previously described, the identification and visualization of the BERTopics is conducted through three functions of the text package: 1) textTopics(), which leverages a pretrained Large Language Models to generate topic representations of the text (here, the essays), 2) textTopicsTest(), which significance tests the topic representations in relation to individuals' characteristics (here, valence), and 3) textTopicsWordcloud(), which visualizes the significant topics.
Except for changing the variable names, the analyses are not adjusted in any other way in comparison to the depression and worry responses.
The textTopics() function generates topic representations of the essays using a pre-trained Large Language Model to transform the essays into high-dimensional embeddings.
Next, the embeddings are reduced in dimensionality and clustered.
For each cluster, the most characteristic words are extracted to produce interpretable topic representations.
The output includes a list of the generated topics (here, 33 topics), including their representations (i.e., the characteristic keywords).

The trained BERTopics model is then submitted to the textTopicsTest() function to perform a significance test of the topic representations relative to the valence scores (here, using linear regression since the target variable is continuous).
The output of this regression are standardized beta coefficients (β) indicating the unique association between each topic and depression severity.
The BERTopics model and statistical test are then submitted to the textTopicsWordcloud() function to visualize the topics.
The output consists of topic word clouds negatively or positively related to valence (as well as non-significant topics).

text.text: The analyses underlying this visualization use word embeddings derived from Large Language Models.
By projecting these embeddings onto a supervised dimension (e.g., low-to-high valence), we visualize which words are most semantically aligned with higher or lower levels of the outcome of interest.

As previously described, the Supervised Dimension Projection plot can be created with three functions of the text package, including 1) textEmbed(), which creates word embeddings of the participants' essays, 2) textProjection(), which preprocesses the data for plotting by creating supervised dimension projections, and 3) textProjectionPlot(), which visualizes the words in the word embedding space.

We transform the essays into word embeddings using the textEmbed() function, which employs a pre-trained Large Language Model to create three types of contextualised embeddings representing the meaning of words in their context: token, text, and word-type embeddings.

To analyze the embeddings in relation to the valence scores, the text and word type embeddings are submitted to the textProjection() function, which creates an embedding that captures the distinction between high and low valence (i.e., the Supervised Dimension Projection).
The preprocessed data is submitted to the textProjectionPlot() function to create the Supervised Dimension Projection plot.
Besides the predefined stopword list (i.e., the snowball lexicon; Porter, 2001), we now also remove punctuations from being plotted ("." and ",").

Specifically, we visualize example responses to the depression and worry questions in relation to a) n-gram user frequencies, b) topic prevalences, and c) language-based assessed valence.

The analyses underlying these visualizations of language examples include identifying the language responses with the highest a) user frequencies of the n-gram "love", b) estimated prevalences of the topic "new", and c) language-based assessed valence.
These examples are identified and visualized using the textExamples() function of the text package.

When identifying language examples from the depression and worry responses in relation to language-based assessed depression severity, we first trained a language-based assessment model using the textEmbed() and textTrain() functions.
We skip these steps here, since the valence scores are already assessed based on the essay language using a pre-trained language-based assessment model from the LBAM library (Nilsson et al., 2025).

text.text: We identify example responses with the textExamples() function.
To a) identify the n-gram example essays, we submit the user frequencies for n-gram "love" from the output of the topicsGrams() function.
To b) identify the topic example essays, we submit the estimated prevalence for the topic "new" from the output of the topicsPreds() function.
The "top terms" list from the topicsmodel() function shows that "new" is topic 22.
To c) identify the language-based assessed valence essays, t he valence scores are submitted.
The n_examples parameter indicates the number of example responses to select.
We decided to select fewer examples (i.e., 3) as compared to the depression and worry responses (i.e., 5) since the essay data contain longer texts, which take up more space in their presentation.
Consequently, three examples resembling the highest, middle, and lowest a) frequencies, b) prevalences, and c) valence are selected (i.e., 9 examples in total for each variable of interest).

The output includes three dataframes with examples of complete responses with the 3 highest, 3 middle, and 3 lowest a) user frequencies of the n-gram "love", b) estimated prevalence of the topic "new", and c) language-based assessed valence.

text.text: Since the essays are longer texts than the depression and worry responses, we 1) selected fewer responses per variable of interest, 2) show the first 80 to 100 words instead of the complete essay, and 3) present them in a table instead of a figure to ensure readability.
We chose a) the n-gram "love", which has been shown to be positively related to valence in the visualization of individual words and phrases (Figure S1).
text.formatted: We chose a) the n-gram "love", which has been shown to be positively related to valence in the visualization of individual words and phrases (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_31">S1</ref>).

text.text: By visualizing the complete responses with the highest user frequency of "love", we can see that they relate to wondering about emotions and relationships (e.g., "How do you know you are in love?") or enjoying hobbies or activities (e.g., "I love doing things like that, but sometimes I give up too easily.").
We chose b) the topic "new", which has been shown to be positively related to valence in the visualization of topics (Figure S4).
text.formatted: We chose b) the topic "new", which has been shown to be positively related to valence in the visualization of topics (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_35">S4</ref>).

text.text: The responses estimated to have the highest prevalence of this topic show it relates to moving, starting college, and meeting new people (e.g., "So, I'm in a new state, in a new place, with no one here that I knew before I arrived").
Finally, the table shows example responses with the highest language-based assess valence (i.e., the essays assessed as including the most positive emotion).
We can see the language includes references to loving a song, remembering good times, loving your family, being excited for college, enjoying the sun, and having special feelings for someone.
These examples align with expectations of language indicative of positive emotion, providing evidence for the face validity of the language-based assessment.

In addition to language-based assessed valence, the essay dataset (Kwantes et al., 2016; Pennebaker & King, 1999) also includes binary variables (0 and 1) for each of the Big Five personality factors (McCrae & John, 1992): Openness (O), Conscientiousness (C), Extraversion (E), Agreeableness (A), and Neuroticism (N).

The final figures in the main manuscript and the supplementary material were accomplished by assembling the visualization components from the functions in R. The visualization components (i.e., word clouds and legends) can be saved and imported into programs of choice, such as PowerPoint or Google Drawings, to combine them and refine the figures and layout.
Here, we provide an example of how you can do this based on Figure 4 (the one-dimensional visualization of LDA topics from the depression and worry phrases in relation to depression severity).

text.text: First, the topicsPlot() function includes parameters to save the visualization components in a specific format.
You can indicate the directory where you want to save the output with the save_dir parameter, and the format (e.g., "svg" or "png") with the figure_format parameter.
It is also possible to save the output in the "plots" screen in RStudio (e.g., as SVG, PNG, TIFF, or PDF).
Then you can upload the components to, for example, Google Drawings.
The screenshot below shows how we first imported the legends and drew an x-axis, including titles.
We then uploaded the topic word clouds and placed them relative to the dot legend.

Next, we added the standardized beta coefficient (β), indicating the strength and direction of association between each topic and depression severity, and added lines to clarify which topic belongs to which dot in the legend.
The size of the standardized beta coefficients and adjusted p-values can be found in the output of topicsTest().
Finally, the final figure can then be downloaded in a format suitable for its final location, such as SVG, PNG, TIFF, or PDF.
The visualizations in this paper are in TIFF format, as it works well for more complex visualizations and prevents quality loss during transfer to publication.
